On grid

An on-grid (or grid-tied) solar system operates in direct synchronization with the local utility 
grid, allowing a facility to generate its own renewable power while relying on the grid for 
backup and banking excess energy. This is the most cost-effective architecture for both kW-
scale residential setups and MW-scale commercial power plants. 
1. Website Write-Up: How On-Grid Solar Works 
The core advantage of an on-grid system is seamless power management without the need 
for expensive battery storage. 
When sunlight hits the solar arrays, the system generates Direct Current (DC) electricity. This 
power immediately flows to the on-grid inverter, which acts as the brain of the system. The 
inverter converts the DC power into grid-compliant Alternating Current (AC) power and 
synchronizes the voltage and frequency with the local utility grid. 
Operating 
Phase 
System Behavior 
Peak Sun 
(Surplus 
Power) 
The solar plant generates more power than the facility is 
consuming. The inverter feeds this excess energy back into 
the utility grid. The bi-directional "Net Meter" spins 
backward, banking credits for the facility. 
Low Sun 
(Deficit 
Power) 
During heavy cloud cover or nighttime, the solar arrays 
underproduce or stop generating. The facility seamlessly 
draws the required power from the utility grid, utilizing the 
banked credits. 
Grid Outage 
For safety reasons, the inverter features "Anti-Islanding" 
protection. If the utility grid fails, the solar system 
automatically shuts down to prevent back-feeding live

Off grid 
 
- The defining characteristic of an off-grid system is its self-reliance, 
achieved through a robust energy storage system. 
- Without the ability to bank excess energy with the grid, an off-grid system 
requires batteries to store solar energy generated during the day for use at 
night or during cloudy weather. This makes the system more complex and 
expensive but offers full autonomy from utility providers and outages. 
Operating Phase System Behavior 
Peak Sun 
(Generation & 
Storage) 
Solar panels generate DC electricity. A "Charge 
Controller" manages the flow of this power, prioritizing: 
1) powering direct DC loads, 2) charging the battery 
bank, and 3) supplying the inverter to power AC loads. 
Nighttime / Low 
Sun (Discharging) 
When solar generation is insufficient, the system 
automatically draws stored DC electricity from the 
battery bank. The "Off-Grid Inverter" converts this 
battery power into AC electricity for the facility's 
appliances. 
Backup / 
Supplementary 
Power 
To ensure reliability during extended periods of low sun, 
most off-grid systems incorporate a backup "Fuel 
Generator" (e.g., diesel or propane). The off-grid 
inverter can start the generator automatically to power 
loads and recharge the batteries.

Hybrid systems – 
 
A hybrid solar system connects to the utility grid but also includes a battery bank to store 
excess energy. This architecture ensures that the energy produced during the day is 
available during nighttime or grid outages, offering greater energy independence. Because 
it remains connected to the grid, it does not require adding an oversized solar array for full 
autonomy, making it more cost-effective than a purely off-grid system. 
Operating 
Phase 
System Behavior 
Peak 
Generation 
Solar panels generate Direct Current (DC) electricity. The 
central hybrid inverter routes this power to run the facility's 
active loads first. 
Energy 
Storage 
Once the facility's immediate power needs are met, excess 
DC power is directed to charge the battery bank for later 
use. 
Grid Export 
If the batteries reach full capacity and the system is still 
producing excess power, the surplus is exported to the 
utility grid for electricity credits. 
Grid Outage 
During power cuts, the system instantly draws from the 
stored battery backup, ensuring an uninterrupted power 
supply.

Ground mounted – 
 
Ground-Mounted Solar Power Plants 
Engineering large-scale solar power plants for reliable, long-term energy generation 
Ground-mounted solar power plants are utility-scale photovoltaic systems designed to 
generate electricity on open land and supply power to industries, commercial facilities, 
institutions, utilities or the grid. 
At MW scale, a solar plant is much more than an installation of solar modules. It is a 
complete electrical and civil infrastructure project involving site engineering, solar 
resource assessment, module selection, mounting structures, DC and AC systems, 
inverters, transformers, protection systems, evacuation infrastructure, SCADA and 
monitoring, testing and commissioning. 
At Urja Solutions, our approach is to engineer every part of the plant with long-term 
performance, safety, reliability and maintainability in mind. 
100+ MW of solar projects executed | MW-scale EPC capability | Engineering-driven 
execution 
 
How a MW-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Plant Works 
A simplified energy flow through a ground-mounted solar plant is: 
SUNLIGHT 
↓ 
PV MODULES 
↓ 
DC STRINGS 
↓ 
STRING / CENTRAL INVERTERS 
↓ 
AC COLLECTION SYSTEM 
↓

STEP-UP TRANSFORMER 
↓ 
HT SWITCHGEAR / SUBSTATION 
↓ 
GRID / CUSTOMER LOAD 
The photovoltaic modules convert sunlight into DC electricity. Multiple modules are 
connected together to form strings, and multiple strings are combined into the plant's 
electrical architecture. 
Inverters convert the DC electricity into AC electricity. The AC power is then collected, 
stepped up to the required voltage through transformers and transferred through the 
plant's HT system to the designated point of interconnection or customer load. 
For a large plant, this process is continuously monitored through SCADA and plant 
monitoring systems, allowing operators to track generation, inverter performance, alarms, 
electrical parameters and plant availability. 
 
1. Site Assessment & Solar Resource Analysis 
A successful MW-scale solar project starts before any structure is installed. 
Our engineering team evaluates the site for: 
 Land availability and usable area 
 Solar irradiation 
 Topography and terrain 
 Contouring and elevation differences 
 Soil conditions 
 Geotechnical characteristics 
 Flood and waterlogging risk 
 Drainage requirements 
 Access roads 
 Internal roads 
 Transmission-line proximity 
 Grid connectivity 
 Shadow analysis 
 Environmental conditions 
 Wind loading 
 Corrosion conditions 
 Water availability for cleaning 
 Construction logistics 
The objective is not simply to fit maximum panels into the available land. 
The objective is to achieve the best balance between installed capacity, energy yield, civil 
works, electrical losses, construction cost, maintainability and long-term reliability. 
 
2. Solar PV Module Selection 
Modules are the primary energy-generating components of the plant. 
At MW scale, module selection should consider much more than the nameplate wattage. 
Important parameters include: 
 Module technology 
 Module efficiency 
 Temperature coefficient 
 Bifacial performance where applicable

 Degradation characteristics 
 Mechanical load rating 
 PID resistance 
 LID / LeTID characteristics 
 Warranty conditions 
 Manufacturing quality 
 Cell and module reliability 
 Availability of the selected model 
 Compatibility with the inverter 
 Site-specific environmental conditions 
For applicable projects in India, module eligibility and regulatory requirements also need 
to be considered. MNRE maintains the Approved Models and Manufacturers of Solar PV 
Modules (ALMM), with applicability depending on the project category. 
At Urja Solutions, we don't select a module simply because it has the highest wattage. We 
look at the complete system and the expected real-world energy performance. 
 
3. Module Mounting Structure 
The mounting structure is the backbone of a ground-mounted solar plant. 
Thousands of modules have to remain correctly positioned for decades while being 
exposed to: 
 Wind 
 Rain 
 Temperature variations 
 UV radiation 
 Corrosion 
 Soil movement 
 Mechanical loads 
The structure therefore needs proper engineering rather than simply being fabricated to a 
standard size. 
Design considerations include: 
Structural design → soil conditions → foundation design → wind loading → module 
configuration → tilt angle → row spacing → corrosion protection → drainage → 
accessibility 
Proper alignment is also extremely important. 
Even relatively small variations in module orientation or table alignment can affect the 
consistency of the array. 
For example, Indian MNRE project specifications commonly require mounting structures to 
be engineered for site-specific wind conditions and corrosion protection, with controlled 
module inclination and alignment. 
 
4. DC Side – Converting Sunlight into Usable Electrical Power 
Individual PV modules generate DC electricity. 
Modules are connected in series to form strings. 
Multiple strings are then connected to the inverter architecture through appropriate DC 
protection and switching arrangements. 
A simplified arrangement is: 
Module → Module → Module → Module 
↓

PV String 
↓ 
DC Protection / Combiner Arrangement 
↓ 
Inverter 
At MW scale, DC design becomes extremely important because poor cable selection, 
excessive cable lengths, bad connections, incorrect string configuration or poor installation 
practices can result in energy losses and reliability problems. 
Our EPC approach focuses on: 
 Correct string sizing 
 Voltage and current calculations 
 Cable sizing 
 Voltage-drop control 
 Connector compatibility 
 Cable routing 
 Cable protection 
 Proper termination 
 Polarity verification 
 Insulation testing 
 Earthing 
 DC surge protection 
 
5. Inverters – Converting DC into AC 
The inverter is the heart of the electrical conversion system. 
It converts the DC electricity produced by the PV array into grid-compatible AC electricity. 
Depending on the plant architecture, the project may use: 
 String inverters 
 Central inverters 
 Distributed inverter architecture 
Inverter selection depends on: 
 Plant capacity 
 Module configuration 
 DC/AC ratio 
 Grid requirements 
 Environmental conditions 
 Operating temperature 
 Maintenance strategy 
 Availability 
 Monitoring requirements 
 Project economics 
At MW scale, inverter performance directly affects plant availability and energy 
generation. 
Therefore, choosing an inverter is not simply about comparing efficiency percentages on a 
datasheet. 
System compatibility, thermal performance, service support, reliability and long-term 
operating conditions matter equally. 
 
6. AC Collection System

The AC output from multiple inverters is collected and transferred through the plant's AC 
network. 
The system can include: 
Inverter → ACDB / Collection Panel → LT/HT System → Transformer 
Protection systems are incorporated to safely isolate faults and protect equipment. 
Depending on plant architecture, this can involve: 
 AC distribution panels 
 HT panels 
 Circuit breakers 
 Protection relays 
 CTs and PTs 
 Surge protection 
 Metering 
 Earthing 
 Auxiliary systems 
Every component needs to be correctly coordinated. 
 
7. Transformer & Voltage Step-Up 
Solar inverters generally produce power at a lower AC voltage. 
For transmission to the plant's interconnection point, the voltage is stepped up using 
transformers. 
For example: 
Inverter output 
↓ 
Low Voltage / Medium Voltage Collection 
↓ 
Step-Up Transformer 
↓ 
HT Voltage 
↓ 
Switchyard / Grid Interconnection 
Transformer selection must consider: 
 Plant capacity 
 Voltage ratio 
 Losses 
 Temperature rise 
 Insulation 
 Protection 
 Cooling 
 Harmonics 
 Site conditions 
 Utility requirements 
A transformer is a major long-term asset, so quality and correct sizing are critical. 
 
8. HT System & Grid Evacuation 
Once the power reaches the required voltage level, it is transferred through the plant's HT 
infrastructure toward the point of interconnection. 
This may include:

 HT switchgear 
 Protection relays 
 Metering 
 CT/PT systems 
 Lightning protection 
 Earthing grid 
 Switchyard 
 Transmission line 
 Grid interconnection equipment 
The plant must also comply with applicable grid requirements and the specific 
interconnection conditions defined for the project. 
 
9. SCADA & Real-Time Monitoring 
A modern MW-scale solar plant needs continuous monitoring. 
SCADA allows the plant operator to monitor parameters such as: 
 Instantaneous generation 
 Daily generation 
 Inverter status 
 String/inverter performance 
 Voltage 
 Current 
 Frequency 
 Power factor 
 Plant availability 
 Alarms 
 Grid status 
 Historical generation 
 Performance trends 
Large and complex PV plants require increasingly comprehensive monitoring because 
faults and underperformance need to be detected quickly. IEA PVPS specifically highlights 
monitoring, data collection and predictive maintenance as important elements of modern 
PV plant operation. 
 
10. Testing & Commissioning 
A solar plant should not be considered complete merely because all modules are installed. 
Before commissioning, the plant needs systematic testing. 
This can include: 
Visual inspection 
↓ 
Mechanical inspection 
↓ 
DC testing 
↓ 
Insulation testing 
↓ 
Polarity verification 
↓ 
String testing

↓ 
Inverter testing 
↓ 
AC testing 
↓ 
Protection testing 
↓ 
Transformer testing 
↓ 
HT testing 
↓ 
SCADA verification 
↓ 
Grid synchronization 
↓ 
Performance verification 
This is where EPC workmanship becomes extremely important. 
 
Why Quality Matters in a MW Solar Plant 
A solar plant is expected to operate for decades. 
A small mistake repeated across thousands of modules can become a major financial issue. 
For example: 
Poor connector installation 
→ Higher resistance 
→ Heating 
→ Electrical losses 
→ Possible failure 
Poor cable management 
→ Mechanical damage 
→ Water ingress 
→ Insulation failure 
→ Downtime 
Poor structure quality 
→ Misalignment / corrosion 
→ Mechanical instability 
→ Maintenance problems 
Poor drainage 
→ Waterlogging 
→ Foundation problems 
→ Access difficulties 
Poor module selection 
→ Higher degradation / reliability risk 
→ Lower long-term generation 
Poor monitoring 
→ Fault remains undetected 
→ Longer downtime 
→ Lost generation

This is why quality should be controlled throughout the EPC lifecycle, not inspected only 
after construction. 
IEA PVPS' 2026 work on PV project decisions specifically emphasizes that quality 
management throughout the PV value chain can reduce downstream failures and create 
measurable economic value. 
 
Real-World Generation Depends on More Than Module Wattage 
A 640 W or 650 W module does not automatically mean the plant will generate a certain 
number of units every day. 
Actual generation depends on: 
Solar irradiation 
 Module performance 
 Temperature 
 Soiling 
 Shading 
 DC losses 
 Inverter efficiency 
 AC losses 
 Transformer losses 
 Grid availability 
 Plant availability 
 Curtailment 
 O&M quality 
This is why we focus on system-level performance rather than simply selling high-wattage 
modules. 
Soiling alone can have a significant impact on energy yield; IEA PVPS identifies soiling as 
one of the major causes of PV underperformance and recommends site-specific monitoring 
and mitigation strategies.

(Introduction) Are you looking for a more reliable and resilient renewable energy solution? 
Traditional standalone solar or wind systems are great, but they are subject to weather

variability. A Wind-Solar Hybrid System combines the best of both worlds, offering a 
consistent and dependable power supply. Let's explore how these systems work, why you 
should consider one, and the key requirements for a successful installation. 
(What is a Wind-Solar Hybrid System?) A Wind-Solar Hybrid System integrates a solar 
photovoltaic (PV) array with a wind turbine, connecting them to a unified battery storage 
system or an electricity grid. This synergy optimizes energy production. Solar panels 
generate electricity during sunny days, and wind turbines generate electricity during windy 
nights or cloudy, overcast days, ensuring a continuous power supply. 
(Benefits of Wind-Solar Hybrid Systems) 
 Higher Energy Yield & Greater Reliability: By combining two complimentary energy 
sources, hybrid systems significantly reduce reliance on a single weather condition, 
providing a more continuous and reliable power output throughout the year. 
 Optimized Land/Space Use: Utilizing both vertical (wind turbine) and horizontal (solar 
panels) space efficiency is a hallmark of hybrid systems. 
 Grid Independence or Support: For off-grid applications, it provides true independence. For 
grid-tied systems, it acts as a robust backup and can sell excess energy back. 
 Environmental Responsibility: Reduce your carbon footprint and rely less on fossil fuels by 
generating clean, renewable energy. 
 Cost Efficiency Over Time: While the initial investment might be higher, the long-term 
energy savings and reduced operational costs make it a financially sound choice. 
2. Requirements to Check Before Installing a Wind-Solar Hybrid System 
When considering a Wind-Solar Hybrid System, several crucial factors must be assessed to 
ensure its feasibility and optimal performance. Here's a comprehensive checklist: 
1. Site Assessment (The Foundation of Success): 
o Wind Speed Profile: Accurate, long-term wind speed data (preferably measured at 
the proposed hub height) is essential. Low or inconsistent wind speeds will render 
the turbine inefficient. 
o Solar Irradiance: Assess the average daily and seasonal solar radiation (often called 
"sun hours") at your location. Shading from buildings, trees, or geographical 
features must be minimized. 
o Land Area & Local Conditions: Ensure adequate space is available for both the solar 
array and the wind turbine tower. Analyze soil composition and terrain to 
determine the appropriate foundation type for the turbine. 
2. Resource Availability & Consistency: 
o Determine if the wind and solar resources at your site complement each other. 
Ideal scenarios often include strong daytime sun and significant nocturnal wind, or 
seasons where one resource is abundant while the other is less so. 
3. Local Regulations & Permitting: 
o Zoning Bylaws: Verify local zoning laws regarding structure heights (for the wind 
turbine tower), setbacks from property lines, and restrictions on solar panel 
installations. 
o Permits: Acquire all necessary permits, which may include building, electrical, and 
environmental permits. Check noise regulations specifically for wind turbines. 
4. Grid Connection (if applicable): 
o Contact your utility company to understand net metering policies, feed-in tariffs, or 
interconnection requirements for feeding excess power back into the grid. 
5. Load Analysis & Sizing:

o A thorough analysis of your energy consumption patterns (peak load and average 
daily usage) is vital. This determines the appropriate size for the wind turbine, 
solar array, and battery bank to meet your specific needs. 
 
 
1. UPS Systems (Uninterruptible Power Supply) 
(Heading: Ensure Business Continuity with UPS Systems) 
(Introduction) In today's digital landscape, power reliability is non-negotiable. Whether it's 
a critical IT data center or industrial automation, a sudden utility outage can cause 
catastrophic data loss, equipment damage, and costly downtime. An Uninterruptible 
Power Supply (UPS) system is your primary defense, acting as a dynamic electrical firewall 
that provides instantaneous, clean backup power when the grid fails. 
(Benefits) 
 Instantaneous Power Backup: Provides seamless, millisecond-level transition to battery 
power during outages, ensuring zero downtime for critical loads. 
 Voltage Regulation & Power Conditioning: Protects sensitive equipment from voltage 
spikes, sags, noise, and frequency variations. 
 Equipment Protection: Acts as a vital buffer, safeguarding delicate electronics and 
machinery from grid instabilities. 
(Typical Applications) 
 Data Centers and IT Server Rooms 
 Healthcare Facilities (Critical Care Units, Imaging Systems) 
 Telecommunications Infrastructure 
 Financial Institutions (Trading Floors, ATMs) 
Requirements to Check (UPS) 
When specifying a UPS system, the following factors are critical: 
1. Load Capacity Analysis: Conduct a comprehensive power audit to determine the total 
connected load (in kW/kVA) and the initial inrush current (the momentary surge from 
motors or large power supplies). 
2. Runtime Requirements: Precisely define how long the UPS needs to provide power during 
an outage. This often dictates the battery bank sizing. 
3. Input Power Quality: Analyze the incoming utility power quality (nominal voltage, stability, 
and reliability) to determine the most suitable UPS topography (Online Double-Conversion, 
Line-Interactive, or Standby). 
4. Redundancy (N+1, N+2, etc.): Assess the criticality of the load. Mission-critical systems 
often require redundant configurations where the failure of one UPS unit doesn't cause a 
total system outage. 
5. Environmental Conditions: Ensure the installation site has proper ventilation, temperature 
control (UPS electronics and batteries are highly temperature-sensitive), and dust control. 
 
 
BESS (Battery Energy Storage Systems) 
(Heading: BESS: The Key to Energy Independence and Grid Stability) 
(Introduction) As the world transitions to renewable energy, grid flexibility and reliability 
are becoming paramount. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are the pivotal 
technology enabling this shift. A BESS captures energy from various sources (solar, wind,

grid) and stores it for deployment when needed. For utilities, it’s a tool for peak shaving; 
for businesses, it offers a path to energy cost optimization and true resilience. 
(Benefits) 
 Load Shifting / Arbitrage: Store inexpensive electricity (e.g., produced during low-demand 
periods by renewables or at night) and use or sell it when electricity prices are peak. 
 Peak Shaving / Demand Charge Management: Drastically reduce utility bills for commercial 
and industrial users by reducing peak demand charges through strategically deploying 
stored energy. 
 Grid Services (Ancillary Services): Provide utilities with fast-response frequency regulation, 
voltage support, and synthetic inertia, enhancing grid stability. 
 Renewable Integration & Stability: Firm up intermittent output from wind and solar farms, 
providing a smooth, reliable generation profile. 
(Typical Applications) 
 Commercial & Industrial (C&I) Peak Shaving 
 Utility-Scale Grid Stability (Frequency Response) 
 Microgrids (Off-grid resilience, community power) 
 Renewable Co-location (Wind+Storage, Solar+Storage) 
Requirements to Check (BESS) 
The complex nature of BESS requires careful planning: 
1. Comprehensive Energy Use Analysis: Perform a detailed energy profile study, identifying 
daily and seasonal peak loads, average consumption, and the primary objective of the 
BESS (e.g., peak shaving vs. 24/7 backup). 
2. Space and Permitting: Secure significant physical space for the battery containers, power 
conditioning systems (PCS), and transformer stations. Zoning and environmental permits 
(specifically regarding fire safety and hazardous materials) are major hurdles. 
3. Battery Technology Selection (Chemistry): Choose the optimal cell chemistry (e.g., Lithium-
ion NMC or LFP , Lead-acid, Flow batteries) based on needed cycle life, safety profile, 
discharge rates, energy density, and cost. 
4. Grid Interconnection Study: For large-scale BESS, a utility grid connection study is essential 
to ensure the grid can handle the power flows (import/export) and to define protective 
relaying requirements. 
5. Thermal Management: Validate that the system has an engineered active cooling or HVAC 
system, as battery life and safety are highly dependent on operating temperature. 
 
 
Comprehensive Battery Solutions 
(Heading: Custom Battery Solutions: Powering Your Innovation) 
(Introduction) While standard battery systems exist, many advanced and specific 
applications require tailored, application-specific energy storage. Our comprehensive 
battery solutions offer specialized engineering and design for everything from lightweight 
medical devices and robust industrial robotics to large-scale, off-grid power systems. We

(Benefits) 
 Application Optimization: The entire system—chemistry, BMS, and packaging—is 
customized for your specific power, runtime, and environmental constraints.

 Chemistry Specificity: Choose from advanced technologies (Lead-Carbon, Gel, Li-Ion, Flow) 
based on whether your priority is extreme cycle life, depth of discharge, temperature 
range, or safety. 
 Integrated Solutions: We don't just supply batteries; we provide fully integrated solutions 
including advanced Battery Management Systems (BMS), thermal solutions, and 
communication protocols. 
(Typical Applications) 
 Telecommunications (Remote Base Stations) 
 Transportation (Electric Vehicle Fleets, AGVs, Mass Transit) 
 Medical Device Backup 
 Off-Grid Village Power & Microgrids 
 Niche Industrial Machinery (Explosion-Proof, Extreme Temps) 
Requirements to Check (Battery Solutions) 
Designing a specific battery solution starts with these variables: 
1. Detailed Load Profile: Define the specific electrical parameters the solution must support: 
constant power (W), constant current (A), peak current duration, average daily energy 
(kWh), and expected depth of discharge (DoD). 
2. Environmental Operational Conditions: Specify the operating and storage temperature 
range, humidity, vibration profile, shock requirements, and altitude (for aviation). 
3. Cycle Life and Longevity: Determine the minimum required calendar life (e.g., 5-10 years) 
and the number of charge/discharge cycles needed to make the project economically 
viable. 
4. BMS Functional Safety: Integrate an advanced Battery Management System (BMS) with 
specific protection functions for cell monitoring, state-of-charge (SoC) and state-of-health 
(SoH) calculation, cell balancing, and communication interfaces. 
5. Safety and Compliance Standards: Ensure the final solution meets all mandatory safety 
certifications (e.g., UL, CE, IEC, UN38.3) required for deployment and transportation. 
 
 
Servo Controlled Voltage Stabilizers (SCVS) 
(Heading: Dynamic Voltage Correction with Servo Controlled Stabilizers) 
(Introduction) While a UPS is vital for total power outages, a much more frequent power 
quality issue is the constant fluctuation of the input utility voltage. Chronic low voltage 
(sags) or high voltage (swells) can reduce the lifespan of electric motors, cause 
malfunctions in CNC machines, and disrupt sensitive testing equipment. A Servo Controlled 
Voltage Stabilizer (SCVS) provides precise, high-speed, and linear correction, maintaining a 
constant, stabilized output voltage. 
(Benefits) 
 Continuous, High-Precision Stabilization: Maintains a tightly regulated output (often within 
±0.5% to ±1.0%) regardless of input voltage variations (sags, swells, or unbalanced phases). 
 Protection for Sensitive, High-Current Equipment: Essential for safeguarding equipment 
that uses large AC motors or sophisticated electronics from voltage instabilities. 
 High Efficiency & Zero Waveform Distortion: Unlike traditional tap-changing stabilizers, 
servo systems are highly efficient and maintain a pure sine wave without introducing 
harmonics. 
 Fast Correction Speed: Provides rapid, high-torque correction using a servo motor to adjust 
a variac/autotransformer.

(Typical Applications) 
 Industrial Facilities (CNC Machines, Printing Presses, Manufacturing Lines) 
 Medical Imaging (MRI, CT Scanners) 
 HVAC and Refrigeration Systems 
 Commercial Buildings with Fluctuating Utility Feeds 
Requirements to Check (SCVS) 
Selecting an SCVS focuses on correction range and capacity: 
1. Input Voltage Fluctuation Range: Accurately map the full range of input voltage 
fluctuations at the site (e.g., +/- 15%, +/- 20%). The SCVS must have a rated correction 
range that exceeds the worst-case fluctuations. 
2. Output Voltage Precision (Accuracy): Define the required output voltage accuracy (e.g., +/- 
1%, +/- 2%). Higher precision is required for CNC or medical equipment. 
3. KVA Capacity (Total Connected Load): Sizing is critical. Conduct a comprehensive power 
audit to calculate the total continuous load (in KVA) and the inrush current requirements, 
ensuring significant headroom (25-30% is standard practice) for future expansion and large 
motor starting currents. 
4. Correction Response Speed: Evaluate the maximum speed of voltage changes at your site. 
A faster response (in V/sec) ensures critical equipment is protected during rapid voltage 
shifts. 
5. Phase Configuration and Balance: Verify whether the load requires a Single-Phase or 
Three-Phase stabilizer. For Three-Phase loads, confirm if the phases are generally balanced, 
or if a stabilizer with independent phase correction is needed to rectify severe imbalances.

1. Solar Pumping Systems 
Website Write-up: Reliable Irrigation & Water Supply Powered by the Sun 
Heading: Sustainable Water Management: High-Efficiency Solar Water Pumping Solutions 
Introduction: 
Unreliable grid electricity and fluctuating diesel costs make continuous water supply a 
constant challenge for agriculture, livestock, rural drinking projects, and industrial setups. 
Solar Water Pumping Systems offer a clean, reliable, and maintenance-free alternative by 
directly converting sunlight into hydraulic power. Utilizing high-efficiency Variable 
Frequency Drives (VFDs) or Solar Pump Controllers, these systems adjust motor speed in 
real time based on solar irradiance, ensuring consistent water delivery from morning till 
evening without recurring fuel expenses. 
Key Benefits: 
 Zero Fuel Costs & Grid Independence: Completely eliminates monthly electricity bills or 
diesel generator expenses. 
 Smart Flow Modulation (MPPT Control): Advanced solar pump drives use Maximum Power 
Point Tracking (MPPT) to pump water even during low-light, cloudy morning and late 
afternoon hours. 
 Low Maintenance & Long Operating Life: Brushless DC (BLDC) or AC submersible motors 
feature robust construction with minimal moving parts compared to combustion engines. 
 Dual Supply Capability: Modern hybrid solar pump controllers can accept both solar DC 
and auxiliary grid/generator AC inputs for round-the-clock emergency pumping. 
Typical Applications: 
 Agricultural Irrigation (Drip, Sprinkler, and Flood) 
 Borewell / Deep Well Extraction & Canal Lifting 
 Rural Community Drinking Water Schemes & Overhead Storage Tanks 
 Commercial Farms, Dairy, and Livestock Watering 
Site & Technical Requirements Checklist (Solar Pumping) 
1. Total Dynamic Head (TDH): 
o Determine the total vertical lift: Depth to water level (static head), dynamic 
drawdown during pumping, surface elevation lift to the discharge point, and 
friction losses through piping and bends. 
2. Water Demand & Discharge Rate: 
o Calculate daily water requirements ($m^3/\text{day}$ or Liters Per Day) and peak 
flow rate ($LPM$ / $m^3/\text{hr}$) based on seasonal cropping patterns or tank 
capacity. 
3. Borewell Characteristics: 
o Measure borewell casing diameter (typically 4", 6", or 8") to match pump outer 
dimensions. 
o Verify safe water yield / recharge rate to prevent the pump from dry running. 
4. Pump Type Selection: 
o Submersible Pumps: Ideal for deep borewells and tube wells. 
o Surface / Monoblock Pumps: Best for rivers, open wells, canals, and storage 
sumps. 
5. Solar Array Sizing & Shadow Analysis: 
o Size the PV array with an appropriate safety margin (typically 1.25x to 1.35x the 
motor rating in HP/kW) to ensure adequate starting torque, installed in an 
unshaded area with seasonal tilt optimization.

6. Protection Mechanisms: 
o Ensure dry-run protection sensors (water-level probes), tank-full float switches, 
reverse polarity, and lightning/surge arrestors (SPD) are integrated. 
 
 
 
Solar & Wind Hybrid Street Lighting Systems 
Website Write-up: Reliable Autonomous Outdoor Illumination 
Heading: 24/7 Autonomous Illumination: Solar-Wind Hybrid Street Lighting 
Introduction: 
While standalone solar street lights are effective, prolonged monsoon seasons, fog, and 
overcast days can lead to depleted batteries and blackouts. A Solar and Wind Hybrid Street 
Light integrates a compact, high-efficiency vertical or horizontal wind turbine with a 
monocrystalline solar panel and an intelligent lithium battery pack on a single mast. By 
harnessing daytime solar radiation and diurnal/nocturnal breezes, the system ensures 
autonomous, uninterrupted illumination all year round without grid trenches or utility 
wiring. 
Key Benefits: 
 Continuous Year-Round Lighting: Complementary generation ensures that even during 
extended cloudy or rainy periods, wind energy maintains battery state-of-charge. 
 Zero Operational Cost & Rapid Deployment: Standalone off-grid operation requires no 
underground cabling, trenching, or utility interconnection. 
 Smart Dimming & Extended Battery Life: Integrated Microcontroller (MCU) with PIR 
motion sensing and multi-stage dusk-to-dawn dimming profiles (e.g., 100% brightness for 
high traffic, 30% for quiet night hours). 
 High-Density Lithium Storage: Integrated Lithium Iron Phosphate ($\text{LiFePO}_4$) 
batteries offer 2,000+ deep-discharge cycles and high thermal tolerance compared to 
traditional lead-acid units. 
Typical Applications: 
 Highway, Expressway, and Ring Road Lighting 
 Industrial Campuses, SEZs, and Plant Perimeters

 Coastal Roads, Hill Stations, and Open Rural Corridors 
 Municipal Parks, Smart City Pathways, and Parking Lots 
Site & Technical Requirements Checklist (Hybrid Street Lights) 
1. Wind Regime & Cut-in Speed: 
o Evaluate the site's average wind speed at 6–10 meters. The micro wind turbine 
should have a low cut-in wind speed (typically $1.5 - 2.5\text{ m/s}$) to begin 
generating power in light ambient breezes. 
2. Mast & Structural Foundation: 
o Calculate dynamic wind load resistance (designed to withstand gusts of up to 
$120–150\text{ km/h}$). The pole and anchor-bolt civil foundation must support 
the combined weight and vibration of the turbine, solar panel, and battery 
enclosure. 
3. Turbine Type Selection: 
o Vertical Axis (VAWT): Omnidirectional (captures wind from any angle), silent 
operation, ideal for urban areas with turbulent wind currents. 
o Horizontal Axis (HAWT): Higher aerodynamic efficiency, ideal for open highways, 
coastlines, and long unobstructed roadways. 
4. Photovoltaic Capacity & Orientation: 
o PV module sizing based on local peak sun hours ($P\text{SH}$) and optimal 
geographic tilt to maximize winter/monsoon harvesting. 
5. Autonomy Days & Battery Sizing: 
o The $\text{LiFePO}_4$ battery capacity must be sized for at least 2–3 days of zero 
generation (autonomy) under worst-case weather scenarios. 
6. Controller Logic & Protection: 
o Must include an integrated hybrid charge controller with: 
 Electronic and electromagnetic braking (dump load) to prevent turbine 
overspeed in heavy storms. 
 Overcharge, deep-discharge, and short-circuit protection. 
 Dawn/Dusk automatic detection with progressive brightness staging.
